utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We sit today to hear the final submissions in this case of the Prosecution. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, and good morning. For the record, I'm Chester Stamp, along with Ms. Daniela Kravetz and Ms. Priya Gopalan for the Prosecution and Ms. Line Pedersen is our case manager here to assist us today. I suspect, Your Honours, that this is the last time that I will be formally addressing you on my feet in this trial. It is probably my last appearance if all runs -- goes well, it will be. And I think I would like at the beginning to acknowledge some persons who participated in the running of this case which for me at least personally has been a very major event in my career as counsel. It has been a year and a half since this case commenced. It has been a very efficient and fast-moving case, in my view, it's faster than most. And there are many persons, some here in court, some not here in court, who assisted in making that happen. I'd like to thank my colleagues from the Prosecution side, the lawyers who appeared in court before Your Honours and many other lawyers who did not appear in court but were outside of court preparing the motion, researching, and doing what is necessary for us to come before you to present this case. We are also thankful to the support staffing of the OTP, the trial support section, the language assistants, investigators, analysts, and our interns. We recently completed the job of putting together a pre-trial brief [sic] in which we tried to discuss most of the important evidence in this case, thousands of exhibits and a couple hundred witnesses, and many of them worked way into the night and into the mornings to get it before the Court on time and in very good order and in very good shape I hope Your Honours will find. We could not have proceeded, Your Honours, without the work or the assistance of those who work in court, in the language booths. They had to put up with lawyers who spoke too fast. It seems most times that I was the most culpable or the one who received the most complaints. They had to put up with overall emotional witnesses and their work is much appreciated. The court reporters who recorded the proceedings and produced a transcript so we could review them early. Those in the technical booth also have to be acknowledged because they have assisted us to manage and to use the high level of technology that we have available with us in court. And the members of the Victims and Witnesses Section, the Registry in total. We appreciate their work and I make special mention of those who have worked with us in court as well as those at the Victims and Witnesses Section. Without the witnesses coming, the trial could not proceed and they worked efficiently to bring the witnesses to The Hague so we could move smoothly and to attend to them, attend to their comfort, while they were here in The Hague. I'd like to acknowledge counsel and the parties on the other side. In the course of this case, they have always been very professional in the way they related to us when we had to work together. And finally, I'd like to thank the Chamber for the manner in which you have conducted the trial and the kind courtesies that you have extended to us. I don't know if counsel should have too much useful to say to the Court after a trial that is so long. If we haven't presented the evidence over a year and a half clearly enough for the Court to seize our case, then perhaps it's -- it might be a little bit too late to do anything about that. However, I'll try my best, Your Honours, to make or to deal with one or two issues I think or to -- of importance, go to the core of what Your Honours have to consider as you evaluate the evidence. And I will not deal with the evidence in too much detail. I think that has been dealt with quite comprehensively in the Prosecution's final trial brief and I hope not to and don't intend to repeat that too much. I will just deal with a couple of core issues and I will spend some time dealing with some matters raised in the Defence brief which I believe ought to be met by the Prosecution and before we rest. Your Honours, having failed to resolve the issue of non-violent and violent separatism on the part of the majority Kosovo Albanians in Kosovo and as conditions for continued Serbian rule deteriorated in Kosovo, the leadership of the FRY and Serbia, including politicians, military figures, and the police leadership embarked on a plan to modify the ethnic balance in Kosovo in order to ensure continued Serbian control over that province. This objective was impossible to achieve without resorting to criminal means, that is the forcible expulsion of a substantial part of the Kosovo Albanian population. Those criminal means took the form of a widespread and systematic campaign of terror and violence directed at the Kosovo Albanian population. Various persons, command structures, and entities played different but complementary roles in the execution of the plan and the public security sector of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, which the accused commanded, had a vital role to play. This trial, Your Honours, is not about the crimes of the KLA. There were crimes committed on both sides. It is neither about the larger political issues of the independence or separatism of Kosovo. These are relevant but ancillary issues. This case is about the liability of one of the principal persons responsible for this planned campaign involving specific crimes charged in the indictment. During this case we have heard witnesses and seen documents that revealed Mr. Djordjevic's position and authority at the apex of the public security sector of the MUP and his actions and conduct in that capacity which were in support of the plan. The Defence asserts - and this is one of the main issues in this trial - and they do so at paragraph 311 of the brief and throughout the case that there was no common plan, that the evidence does not amount to an organised campaign but of isolated incidents perpetrated by random individuals. That's what they've said in the brief. This, Your Honours, is an attempt to minimise and localise the crimes that the Chamber have to consider. The plan to expel the Kosovar Albanian population or a substantial portion thereof and to prevent their return is borne-out by the scale of the crimes and the pattern of the crimes, which is discussed at the -- in the final trial brief of the Prosecution from paragraphs 458. Approximately 800.000 Kosovar Albanians were expelled, thousands murdered in less than three months in this relatively small geographical area. One can readily perceive the organised pattern from the crime-base evidence, that is, the evidence of the victims who survived and the observers on the ground. That is what I refer to as crime-base evidence. Typically there were joint VJ and MUP assaults on village -- villages and population centres, and the Kosovo Albanian population was expelled through violence and threats of violence and other persecutory acts. Often the personal identification cards were confiscated and destroyed and their homes destroyed to prevent their return. Sometimes groups of them, mostly men, were separated from the fleeing populace and killed. The Kosovar Albanian population was thoroughly terrorised and this resulted in further mass exodus. The evidence reveals, Your Honour, that practically the same pattern of expulsions was occur -- or were occurring at disparate locations throughout Kosovo and Metohija. It is submitted, respectfully, that the crime-base evidence considered in its entirety is sufficient to prove that there was a widespread and systematic campaign. In addition to this, a finding that there was a widespread and systematic campaign against Kosovar Albanian population is confirmed by the evidence of the clandestine transportation of the bodies of over 800 Kosovar Albanian persons to Serbia proper and their concealment in mass graves. The bodies that were transported to Serbia and buried there to cover up the crimes is, Your Honour -- Your Honours, unchallenged evidence. And the Chamber is entitled to draw certain inferences from this unchallenged evidence. Some of them are pretty obvious, including one that the remains of these victims or these persons were the remains of persons who were victims of murder and that the parties who organised this transshipment and concealment were aware that they were murder victims and not combatants or victims of the accidental killings but murder victims. There must have been awareness of that. And the parties who organised this transshipment and concealment were conscious of their guilt or their participation in these murders; that is, these weren't killings that arose from the activities of the KLA, for example, or ordinary crime. The reasons why the bodies were moved so far and so much resource and effort was put in place to move over 800 bodies, hundreds of miles to be concealed in mass graves must have been because the persons involved in the movement were responsible for these killings. And it is obvious also, I think, that this was the result of high-level planning and organisation. It is manifest that an operation to ship so many bodies so far involving so many people must have been planned very carefully and from a high level. These points again have been set out and the evidence in support of these points have been also been set out in the final trial brief, but these, it is submitted, are clear inferences that the Court is entitled to draw from the mere fact of the transport of these bodies, which is evidence that has not been and indeed cannot be challenged. Another incident -- inference can be drawn from this evidence, Your Honours, an inference and the Prosecution submits the sure inference is that the murders were the consequence of a planned campaign. The sheer scale and number of the victims is proof enough by itself, but this is not the only aspect that the transshipment of the bodies establishes. Careful analysis of the forensic evidence in its entirety of Sterenberg, the forensic archaeologist, the DNA evidence from the ICMP and Dr. Alonso from the Madrid forensic institute, the evidence of Dr. Baraybar, the forensic anthropologist and the OMPF list of missing persons establishes that the human remains of Kosovar Albanians found at the mass graves in Serbia were from many different crimes committed at many different places committed at many different times. The bodies came from a multitude of crime sites all over Serbia -- all over Kosovo, I beg your pardon. And this is overwhelming evidence, it is submitted, of a planned, widespread and systematic campaign, not merely random killings. If it were random, the persons involved in the transit and concealment of the bodies would not know where to gather all of these bodies from all of these crimes. Your Honours, what I'm saying is that these bodies that were found in Serbia were not the -- did not arise from one, two, or three incidents and they were gathered up and hidden, but there were many incidents spreading all over Kosovo, right through the indictment period of reported killings and murders, where all these bodies were gathered up and taken and concealed in Serbia. So it proves more than just scale. It proves more than just planning. It proves, it is submitted by the Prosecution, knowledge of these various murders. P815, that is Exhibit P815, comprises exhumation reports by Sterenberg on behalf of the International Commission of Missing Persons, the ICMP. It details the process of exhumations of the three mass graves at Batajnica, Petrovo Selo and Bajina Basta in the area of Lake Perucac in Serbia where remains of these Kosovar Albanians were found. It tells us that 705 bodies or body parts from 705 individuals at least were found at Batajnica, 75 at Petrovo Selo, and 48 at Bajina Basta. Following DNA analysis conducted by the ICMP and Dr. Alonso in Madrid, the vast majority of these human remains were identified and the ICMP provided us with those -- with the lists of the persons identified which is contained in P818, which I think is before on the screen. And it lists the hundreds of persons whose bodies were identified from the mass graves in Serbia. I'll just -- if we could we just look at one page, perhaps. There are over 600 -- I think it lists 650 persons, Kosovo Albanians, whose bodies were found in this grave. We heard the evidence about the Suva Reka massacre from Shyhrete, Hysni Berisha and Hebib Berisha. These are some of them who were found years later, including babies, at Batajnica. After the completion of the identification procedure, the bodies were returned to the families by the United Nations mission in Kosovo and the cases closed were applicable. P477 is a consolidated list of persons reported missing in Kosovo to the ICRC, that's International Commission of the Red Cross and other international organisations which was consolidated by the UN Office of Missing Persons and Forensic, the OMPF. And importantly, when the ICRC and other bodies recorded the information or the reports of the disappearance of these persons in Kosovo, they also recorded the dates when these persons were recorded as having disappeared and the location of the event where the persons were reported to have disappeared from. I just put it on the screen to remind the Court of this document which is in evidence. You will see in the columns fourth from right or fifth from right, the date of the event and the location of the event where the persons on this list disappeared from. The names on this list, the ICRC list -- the OMPF list of unaccounted persons includes many of those whose remains were identified in mass graves in Serbia, and it demonstrates, Your Honours, that the murders and the violence in Kosovo and Metohija were not random, isolated events but were the result of the execution of a plan. And to give the Chamber a better idea of the widespread and systematic nature of the crimes and the cover-up, I have merged these two exhibits, that is, I have merged the ICMP list of identified victims found in the three mass graves in Serbia with the information from the OMPF and the ICRC, showing the location of the events and the dates of the disappearance. And before you now, Your Honours, there is a consolidated spreadsheet. Happily, the ICRC and OMPF lists were submitted in evidence in spreadsheet formats so the Chamber would be able to do much of what I propose to do. This spreadsheet only includes those cases where the remains were recovered for the mass graves in Serbia and those -- and who were identified and the locations and places where they were killed and disappeared or disappeared were recorded. And what I've done first is assort the sheet by the place of the event of the disappearance of these victims. These are persons, I remind the Court, who were found -- or whose remains were found at Batajnica. If we look at this, scroll down, we see a variety of places, Cabrat, Dardania, Pec, Djakovica, many of these found at Batajnica, Izbica, Skenderaj, Pec, Kacanik, Kosovo Polje, Landovica, Ljubanic, Pec, Meja. There will of course be many from Meja because in one particular incident on the 27th of April, 1999, at least 300 men weaponry murdered and disappeared. Their bodies, this shows were found, at Batajnica. People from the village of Ramoc, Djakovica, Slovinje. We heard a lot of evidence about people being expelled and murdered in these places. If we were to represent what we see here on a map, and this is Annex C, we can't represent each individual killing but we can represent the concentrations of the killings, we see that the bodies found in Serbia came from right across -- from incidents that were reported to have occurred right across Kosovo. There ought to have a bigger circle to the south of the map to represent the Suva Reka massacre, but the Suva Reka massacre on the 25th of March, for some reason, was not reported to the ICRC so it does not come up on their list. So that massacre is not represented here. The ICRC list, Your Honours, is not exhaustive. This just indicates some of the murders and we can have an idea of the spread. Another important matter which the ICRC list can assist the Court with if we analyse it on a spreadsheet is the spread, if we sort it by the date of the killings or the date of the disappearances, we see that the persons whose bodies were found in Serbia were killed over a long period of time right through the indictment period. March, we could probably go quickly; April, different dates in April, different dates in March; May, different dates; 8th of June; and we see one at the bottom, 7th of July. So I should advise the Court that that one is in the ICRC records, a disappearance which -- but I take it Your Honours would understand that in records of this nature that the ICRC would keep -- the odd error would creep in. It does not affect the substance of the records in respect to the killings. One error -- I think an error was made in recording the date, does not affect the record in respect to thousands of people. So, Your Honour, this is not merely, as the Defence suggested in their brief, a massive criminal enterprise, but it is also one of significant complexity. And the recovery and transshipment of the bodies from so many crimes committed at so many or on so many occasions could only have been achieved, it is submitted respectfully, if there was knowledge of these crimes and high-level planning and management. The parties who organised the collection and transfer and concealment of these bodies in Serbia must have had knowledge of these murders as they were ongoing. The collection of the remains of the victims of murder committed on so many different days at these disparate places is clear evidence, it is submitted, of planning and organisation and also of knowledge of the ongoing killings because only persons with the knowledge of the killings from these various places where they occurred would have been able to carry this out. And the Prosecution submit respectfully that the forensic evidence viewed broadly and in its totality entitles the Court to make this finding as a safe and sure finding, not only that it was widespread and systematic but that it was planned. The Defence said at paragraph 308 of its brief that it defies logic that there was a plan, but it is submitted, Your Honours, that this forensic evidence in reality shows that there could be no other logical and reasonable explanation but that there was a plan. There is, if I could move on, an additional question the Chamber could grapple with and it is whether or not there was just a campaign of killings or of persecutions or whether these organised killings, obviously systematic, were also related to the deportations which the Prosecution alleges is the motivation for all of these crimes that were committed against the Kosovar Albanians. The Prosecution submits that the answer to this question could only be yes and that it is a certain and safe conclusion, that if these murders fell within an organised scheme then the related deportations were also organised and planned. Many of the victims, including those referred to in the ICMP report including whose remains were found in mass graves, disappeared from places and at times where according to the evidence tendered in the trials there were mass expulsions of Kosovar Albanians. If we -- and we could look through, and I invite the Court to do so, look through the column for group disappearances and if we sort that by place, these are when the reports of groups having been killed, we see that many of them occurred in places where there were massive deportations of Kosovo Albanians. And if we -- once you scroll down for group deportations you see Izbica, the Izbica killings, massive deportations. The striking one of course is always Meja because there were so many persons killed in the Meja incident, but the evidence of the people who were witnesses to the Meja incident, particularly Pnishi, I hope I got his name right Martin Pnishi, Dedaj, and Nike Peraj told of massive deportations that were associated with the murders that occurred there. And I'll return briefly to the Meja incident when I come to discuss the crime base. But for the time being if I could just remind the Court that the victims of Meja were found at Batajnica. As we are speaking about deaths and evidence of killings, Your Honours, if we could look briefly at Annex C to the -- well, to the proof of death chart, which is annexed to the Prosecution pre-trial brief [sic]. The proof of death chart refers to evidence relevant only to the named victims of murder incidents that are specifically charged in the indictment. The other lists which I just went through deals with -- one list deals with all of the identified victims from the mass graves in Serbia, and the other list, the ICRC list deals with all of the reports that they receive in respect to disappearances. The proof of death chart is more narrow and more specific. It just deals with the names of those who are specifically listed in the indictment for the specific count of murder. The remains of some of these victims, however, were found in the mass graves in Serbia, Suva Reka, in Schedule D of the indictment were found at Batajnica, Izbica; in Schedule F were found at both Batajnica and at Petrovo Selo; and most of the Meja victims were found at Batajnica and Meja is Schedule H. The chart, Your Honour, consolidates in one place for easy reference by the Chamber the evidence in respect to each of these named victims. It is not evidence, but we proffer it as part of the final submissions, and I think it can assist the Court in locating the forensic evidence referred to each of the deceased persons insofar as proof of these specific charges of murder in the indictment is required. And it includes forensic evidence in respect to the examination of those human remains and also the identification evidence, mainly DNA evidence and to some degree the evidence of the murder of these persons. The proof of death chart is not on the screen. I think this is the ICRC chart. When one scrolls through this, one will see that many of the victims or most of the victims were men, which is consistent with the viva voce testimony before the Court, that in the course of these expulsions men were taken away and shot while the rest of the population was expelled. The evidence reveals, as Dr. Baraybar testified, that the vast majority of the scheduled victims of murder whose remains were recovered in a state that was susceptible to forensic examination died from gun-shot wounds inflicted on persons who were not engaged in combat. These were murder victims. Baraybar and his team used the most advanced methodology of forensic anthropology to reach these conclusions as the state of decomposition in many of these bodies was far advanced. There has been some challenge in the course of the trial as to whether or not Dr. Baraybar and his team could make findings on the cause of death, having regard to the state of these human remains. Dr. Baraybar testified before the Court and he told the Court about the modern techniques available in his field to review human remains, particularly bones, and to come to forensic conclusions. I respectfully invite the Chamber to review the proof of death chart, and where there is evidence from viva voce witnesses as well as forensic evidence in respect to a killing or the cause of death, it will become readily apparent to the Court that evidence of the crime-base witnesses with particular killings is materially consistent with the forensic evidence of Dr. Baraybar as well as the evidence presented through Dr. Baccard. I turn now to the issue of the individual criminal liability of the accused as a participant in the plan. So the Prosecution submits, Your Honours, there -- that the evidence establishes that there was a widespread and systematic campaign that was planned, there was a joint criminal enterprise. And it is in the nature of things that this joint criminal enterprise could not have been effected without the participation of the police. Mr. Djordjevic 's knowledge and conduct at all relevant times, as proven by the evidence, establishes his liability as a participant in this plan and also for aiding and abetting the perpetrators of the crimes charged. The evidence discussed in the Prosecution's final trial brief establishes that he knowingly made significant contributions to the joint criminal enterprise and assisted in the commission of the crimes by, among other things, participating in the arming of non-Albanian civilians and disarming Albanian villages; participating in the co-ordination of joint VJ/MUP operations through the Joint Command and the command structure of the police; and in these operations crimes were committed. He authorised, along with Minister Stojiljkovic, the use of paramilitary groups and volunteers, particularly, particularly, the Skorpions which committed many of the crimes charged. And he, most tellingly, played a leading role in concealing the crime of murder, concealing the bodies that were located in the mass graves in Serbia. He acted in concert with other persons named in the indictment, but primarily with the minister of interior, Minister Stojiljkovic. Your Honours, although the Defence, particularly the accused in his testimony, would invite the Court to come to a view that there was tension and disagreement between the accused and his minister at the relevant time and the accused was not in agreement and was not a willing participant in the acts and conduct that led to the police participation in these crimes, it is submitted, Your Honour, that a full examination of the evidence discloses that they worked together, they fit together like hand in glove. And without reviewing all the evidence that we have pointed out, I would respectfully just refer the Court to one series of dispatches by both of them which demonstrates the point that these were not men working and pulling in opposite directions, but they were pulling together. If we look at P85. This is a very important exhibit, Your Honours. This is a record of a meeting of the 17th of February where the plans for the operations during which many of the crimes that we are -- we have to consider were committed were discussed. Present at the meeting was the minister, as one can see; and immediately before him, the accused, Mr. Djordjevic. And if we move to page 3, we see at the end of his presentation the minister issues the following tasks. It reads: "Our forthcoming tasks are as follows ..." And in the middle of those bullet points, he says: "Approach and engage volunteers carefully, linking their engagement through the reserve police force when assessed as necessary." The next day, on the 18th of February, 1999, Mr. Djordjevic issued the dispatch which is P356. We have the front page before us. If we could move on. We see him at item 7 saying: "Through intensified intelligence and other measures and actions, carry out necessary checks, complete lists, and establish complete control over volunteer and paramilitary units and their members." And if we could go back to the front page of this dispatch, this is dispatch number 312 of the 18th of February, 1999. The plans having been made at around that period -- we move to the 24th of March, 1999, when the -- they were about to be executed. And if we could look at P702, which is a dispatch by the minister. And in the first paragraph of that document we see the minister says: "It is necessary to intensify the enforcement of measures that were ordered as per our dispatch number 312 of the 18th of February, 1999." Clearly, Your Honours, in regard to the engagement of paramilitaries and volunteers, something that led to enormous crimes, Mr. Djordjevic and Mr. Stojiljkovic were pulling in the same direction. It was their dispatch, 312. Having referred to their dispatch, although it was signed by Djordjevic, but their dispatch, the minister says: From that dispatch "you are to enforce in particular the following measures: " Look at paragraph 5: "You shall register all volunteer and paramilitary units and their members and keep them under control in case that you might need to engage them." This seems to have presented some problems for the Defence in writing their pre-trial brief [sic] because I notice their final brief. At paragraphs 102 to 104, they tried to explain away the clear meaning of these words, or I think it's a matter that they have given up trying to explain away the clear meaning of these words. Some Defence witnesses, insiders, subordinates of Mr. Djordjevic, came to tell us that the words he used and the words the minister used did not mean that they were planning to engage paramilitaries and volunteers. Well, we expect that from those witnesses. But what the Defence has argued in their pre-trial brief [sic] now is that the minister was doing one thing and Mr. Djordjevic was doing something else. They say at paragraph 102 that Djordjevic's order, the one that he signed, was aimed at preventing paramilitary and volunteer units from gathering and operating; conversely, the minister was instructing that former volunteer units could possibly be admitted if they met the requirements. Djordjevic, they say, was preventing; the minister was enabling. Well, Your Honours, respectfully, that just doesn't wash. The minister -- the minister's dispatch of whom the first addressee, the man at the top of the list, was Mr. Djordjevic, speaks of "our" dispatch and says to enforce in particular "our" instructions. So they weren't pulling in different directions; they were part of the same team, members of the joint criminal enterprise. That Mr. Djordjevic participated in acts that furthered the joint criminal enterprise, Your Honours, I respectfully submit, is beyond dispute. He participated in the engagement of the Skorpions; that is admitted. We see these documents of him facilitating the engagement of paramilitaries. He was involved and admitted that he hid or participated in concealing several truck-loads, I think at least six truck-loads of bodies of up to 8 -- beyond 800 in Serbia. And these are the bodies of victims of the crimes that we charge. So his participation or acts and conduct that participated to the JCE, it is submitted, are beyond issue in this case. The interesting point or one interesting point in the case and his state of mind, knowledge; when he was doing all of these things, what did he know. The essence of Mr. Djordjevic's defence is that he had no command responsibility for the police in Kosovo. I think we have dispatched that one in the pre-trial brief [sic], and I won't be repeating those arguments here. He had the power, he had the command over them. He had no command responsibilities for those police he's saying, at least those engaged in the anti-terrorist actions. He's saying that he did nothing to contribute to the JCE. I think, Your Honours, that it is clear that the opposite is true. And mainly he's saying that insofar as there were crimes committed, he, as the chief of police, did nothing because apart from the Podujevo incident he knew nothing about these crimes. That is the pith and gravamen of his defence. When I did what I did, I knew nothing about these crimes specifically, I knew nothing or I knew not that these crimes were ongoing. One of the questions for the Chamber, Your Honour, is this: If you accept that there was a campaign, a widespread and systematic campaign of violence, including murders against the Kosovo Albanians with the hundreds of killings and expulsions, did Mr. Djordjevic as chief of the regular police of the country have a duty to act to protect the safety of the endangered population and did he discharge his duty to act in that way or did he, on the other hand, knowingly act to assist and support the campaign? The Prosecution says that not only did he fail in his duty to protect the endangered population, but he actively participated in facilitating the commission of the crimes. One of the critical elements in answering this question is, as I indicated, an analysis of his state of mind at the relevant time. Because if he knew that the crimes were being committed or would be committed when he acted as he did, particularly in concealing the bodies, he's liable for contributing to the joint criminal enterprise and aiding and abetting their commission. The accused elected to testify; that's his right. He probably did so having regard to his rank as chief of the regular police and it was thought that he needed to explain certain things that he did. The Prosecution does not say that he has any obligation to prove or disprove anything, but he has raised a defence and it is for the Trial Chamber to evaluate his testimony and to make of it what you think fit. His defence primarily is that he knew not. In evaluating his testimony, Your Honours, I ask you to bear in mind that the accused is a trained lawyer who spent 30 years in the police force, the last part of which he was in a very powerful position as an assistant minister and chief of the public security section. He said when he testified that at the relevant time he was aware in general terms that there may have been crimes committed somewhere, as every war is accompanied by crime. But apart from Podujevo, he never became aware of specific allegations during the indictment period. He told you, Your Honours, further that he never became aware of specific allegations during the remainder of 1999. He told Your Honours that he never became aware of the allegations against the police force in Kosovo in the year 2000. In his testimony, Your Honours, he told you that in the year 2001 he did not become aware of the allegations against the police force in Kosovo. He said specifically he did not even know about the Suva Reka massacre, a crime for which ultimately a SUP chief would be charged, until many years later when the persons were charged in Belgrade. He never knew about the Mala Krusa massacre of scores of people which was published in the international press at the time and was subject to the indictment made public in May 1999 against his boss, Mr. Stojiljkovic. He never knew about it until 2003 when he got the indictment against him. That is what he told you. And Your Honours will have to consider whether or not you believe that, whether or not, to put it unforensically, whether you can buy that, whether it evokes in your mind reasonable doubt. That perhaps is the best way to put it. Stojiljkovic was indicted for these crimes in 1999, 1999, May 1999. He was burying bodies with Stojiljkovic in May 1999 and he tells the Court that those crimes that Stojiljkovic was indicted for, he did not know about them until 2003. I remind the Court that the bodies found in Batajnica from the evidence were of persons killed right up until the end of May 1999. I'm reminded that the president of the country, Milosevic, was extradited to The Hague to stand trial for some of these charges that he says he never heard about until 2003. Your Honours, I assume that any interested party, any interested party in the world knew about these crimes and it is beyond belief that the former police chief of the country did not know about these crimes. It is beyond belief that when he did what he did he did it in complete ignorance of these crimes. Your Honours, if I may respectfully again go unforensic. I ask the Court not to buy that. He could not have participated as he did and become so deeply involved without knowledge of what he was doing. And, Your Honours, as a matter of fact that doesn't fit the type of persona that all the senior police officers who testified described him as, all internationals who knew him described him as, as a leader of strong decisive personality. That doesn't fit that he would be engaged in these huge crimes of concealing bodies or -- acts, call it that, of concealing bodies in complete ignorance. When he testified, Your Honours, it was to explain the evidence, uncontrovertible evidence, as to what he did. And he was asked some questions, he was asked to explain some things, and in the course of his testimony I submit and I ask you to find, because he could not answer satisfactorily primarily questions about what he knew, he resorted to a defence or a claim that he acted under duress. He found himself in a situation where it became difficult to explain how he could have done what he did and not know what he was doing, and eventually said: Well, I did it because I was -- I feared for my life. He said I -- that he acted as he did because he was afraid for his life because of what he understood to be a serious threat from the minister. He does not know the minister to be a dangerous man, but he knows Serbia to be a dangerous country. This is the police chief giving evidence to you. He says dangerous things were happening in Serbia at the time and he felt afraid because he understood the minister to be threatening him. Your Honours, he tried to explain his conduct and his state of mind to the Court for over one week in his evidence in chief when he was being asked questions by counsel for the Defence, and he was asked many times about his motivation for doing what he did and not once did he say it was because he was afraid. He wrote a letter in June 2004 to the "Nedeljni Telegraf," this is P1474. And it spent pages explaining his motivations. He did not say that he did what he did because he felt threatened for his life. He addressed this Court in his opening speech in January 2009 and he discussed his motivations for doing what he did, for burying these murder victims and concealing the crime of murder. He did not say then that he did it because he was afraid for his life. So Your Honours would have to consider whether he said that during cross-examination because he was being asked hard questions and he reached a point where he could not explain why he did it and he could not explain his state of mind. Besides, Your Honours, we see from the evidence which is discussed in the closing brief that there were some events in October 2000, and he claimed that he was threatened not only by the minister but by two assistant ministers and they tried to force him to resign and they tried to get him to do certain acts that he thought would endanger Serbian lives and he refused, refused to comply with what the minister ordered him to do. That evidence is important for two things, it shows that he could refuse, he could stand up and say no and not commit crimes; but it also shows, Your Honours, that the minister as the political boss of the Ministry of the Interior could not use the police without the participation of Mr. Djordjevic. That is why he had to resign when he refused to do what the minister told him to do. They wanted him to resign, to put in somebody in his place who would comply. That is the most or among the most telling evidence of his power, the power invested in him as chief of the public security sector. The minister couldn't use the police without him. And we see also that even in the Defence brief at paragraph 582 to 583, even the Defence argues that when Djordjevic couldn't put up with the shipment of the bodies anymore, he merely told the minister that it had to stop and it stopped. That is a concession from the Defence. So the defence, if you call it that, of duress of what he did doesn't wash. He knew what he was doing, Your Honours, and he was acting to further the joint criminal enterprise. The Defence at paragraph 427 of the brief alleges that Mr. Djordjevic sought to investigate the issues of bodies even after the war, but the minister prevented him - they said "prevented him," as if the minister could force him, could coerce him. Again, that type of argumentation has no foundation on the evidence, and it is rebutted by the fact that Mr. Djordjevic remained in office for many months after the minister was removed from office. And in that period of time when the minister was out of the way, he did none of the things that he admitted he ought to have done but did not do. Your Honours, I submit respectfully that that -- the evidence shows that he played a voluntary role in furthering these offences. He acted wilfully and voluntarily with knowledge, not under duress, not under coercion. The Trial Chamber is entitled to find that his participation in the concealment of the bodies was voluntary. A Judge of fact can infer knowledge and intent from the voluntary conduct of an accused person. The Trial Chamber is entitled to find from Djordjevic's conduct, particularly his participation in the concealment of the bodies, that there is no other reasonable inference available on the evidence but that he possessed the relevant awareness and intent to further the crimes that were being committed. The bodies were from a continuing campaign of murder right throughout the indictment period, and he was concealing them while the murders were ongoing. He must have known what he was doing. To put it another way, Your Honours, you may conclude that he had sufficient knowledge and intention. If the circumstances in which he engaged in this cover-up were so suspicious and his alleged failure to make inquiries were so clearly deliberate that there is no other reasonable explanation other than he was fully aware of the entire scheme and his role in it. It bears repeating that a man of his stature, a man of it ilk described as he was by so many people, including his former subordinates and the senior internationals who met him, could not have become deeply involved without knowing what he was doing. And the Trial Chamber, it is submitted, should not allow what would appear in his evidence to be his wilful blindness to be an avenue for escaping liability of participation in the JCE and aiding and abetting the perpetrators. And it is to be noted, Your Honours, having regard to the charts I showed you, that had he acted appropriately on the first occasion when he became aware of these murders -- of these bodies, it is unlikely, nearly impossible, impossible, that the remaining murders would have been committed. Had he done just one or two things in his capacity as chief of police for the country to discharge his responsibility, to protect the endangered population, thousands would be alive. There are other areas, if I may move on, it is respectfully submitted, other areas of his testimony that the Court may well find raises grave concerns about his sincerity when he testified. Mr. Djordjevic gave different accounts about what happened after the discovery of the corpses, and I'll read them quickly as I see time is moving quickly -- quicker than I am. In his letter of June 2004 to the "Nedeljni Telegraf," P1474, he said when he got the call from Mr. Golubovic: "I immediately proposed that the complete criminal process be conducted there. Immediately after that conversation, I informed the minister about everything and a half hour later, he issued an order for me for the bodies to be transported to Belgrade for autopsy and further processing." In his opening statement he told the Court: "I thought that the regular police crime investigation had to be carried out in accordance with the law and this is what I insisted on in my conversation with the chief of the SUP in Bor; however, having received additional information and in light of the fact that the local SUP could not do this in accordance with the procedure, I informed the minister about all that and he took all the decisions that followed." So he's out of it, having informed the minister. When he testified he gave a third account as to what he did immediately upon hearing about these bodies. He said that the order of the minister -- that he went to the minister immediately and that the order of the minister was that after routine procedures the bodies should be buried in the vicinity where they were found. He sought to explain away these contradictory statements by saying that in his previous renditions he left things out or he wasn't being accurate, but that his testimony was to be believed because he was being complete and accurate in his testimony. Mr. Djordjevic in the course of this trial testified at another war crimes trial by videolink, and we saw his testimony in that case. It's P1508. He told the Judges in that trial in respect to the important issue as to his whereabouts in Kosovo in 1999, he said he was in Kosovo only once in 1999 along with the minister. He misled the Chamber because we know from the evidence here, which he accepts, that he was there several times in 1999. When I put to him that he had recently misled another Trial Chamber when giving evidence, he said that what he told them there was probably a mistake. This is at transcript 9970 of the 10th of December, last year. What he told them was a mistake but he insisted what he was telling you was the truth. It's a matter for you. It's a matter for you as to whether that type of error making causes you grave concerns about his sincerity when he testified. Your Honour, we have testimony about the circumstances in which he ended his career in the police force. He said that he fled Serbia when he became aware that a criminal report had been filed against him for abuse of office and that it was not because of his involvement in the bodies' concealment. Your Honours will have to consider what were the real reasons for his flight, for the ending of his career in the police force so precipitously -- I think so precipitately and his sudden departure from his homeland. Because flight can be evidence of a guilty mind and it is for the Tribunal of fact, at the end of the day, to consider whether there is any other reasonable explanation for flight, apart from knowledge of guilt. Is it a coincidence that just when the news regarding the find of the mass graves at Batajnica was brewing in the media in Serbia, just about that time he disappeared? Or is it because of this investigation for abuse of office? K84, (redacted) (redacted) received certain information and spoke to Mr. Djordjevic about it at the initial stages of his investigation. At that time Mr. Djordjevic was still in Serbia. Mr. Djordjevic told him what happened happened, and that was the end of the conversation. You recall these were two senior policemen who had known each other right throughout their careers. This is not something that is a regular event in the police force in Serbia or anywhere in the world, that in the -- just on the outskirts of the capital hundreds of bodies are found in a mass grave. Djordjevic's response: What happened happened. He did not give K84 any assistance apart from that, nothing, not a word, not a word did he tell K84 about what he came to this trial to tell this Trial Chamber. When the Working Group sought to interview him again, they could no longer locate him and Mr. Djordjevic was declared a wanted person by the police so he could be brought in for questioning. I ask Your Honours to recall the evidence that while the -- the new about the find of the mass graves was breaking, and shortly after what Mr. Djordjevic described at his retirement, he met with Mr. Lukic and K83. K83 was one of the drivers of the trucks that was shipping the bodies from Serb -- from Kosovo to be concealed in Serbia. He met with Lukic and K83 during that period -- sorry, K93. And it was decided that K93 would be transferred away from Belgrade to work in a town on the other side of the country away from the spotlight. Djordjevic could find time to meet with Mr. Lukic for that purpose, but he couldn't find time to tell the investigator, K84, who was investigating the bodies, what he came to tell us. He couldn't find time to write a letter to say: This might assist you in your investigations. He could find time to continue a cover-up. Djordjevic's suggestion, if I could just add, in explaining this meeting with Lukic and K93, he said that he just happened to be back in the building as a pensioner and dropped in Lukic's office when the meeting took place is really very, very strange because he also tells us that it was Lukic who was the one who called him in and gave him his letter of retirement to sign against his will. So his explanation as to how he came to be in Lukic's office is unusual, to say the least, but the fact is that the testimony is that in that office at that time it was decided to transfer away from Belgrade, away from the spotlight, one of the truck drivers. And after that, Djordjevic fled Belgrade and remained a fugitive until 2007. Djordjevic went to great lengths -- perhaps, Your Honours, it is time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is indeed, Mr. Stamp. We will have the break now and resume at 11.00, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. In explaining how he came to end his career in the police force, Mr. Djordjevic during his examination-in-chief said that he was dismissed from the police force on the 3rd of May, 2001. Later on, when he was presented with his request for retirement, he changed his testimony, saying that he was retired on the basis of his request not dismissed. His evidence became that he was retired without his knowledge. He says that he was summoned to Mr. Lukic's office on the 4th of May, where a request for early retirement already written up was presented to him and he simply signed it. The cross-examination he was asked why he signed. He said he did not want to cause any problems. If the state had decided to retire him, he was willing to accept it. And this is what -- or how, according to him, he would have the accord to believe his 30-plus-year career in the police force ended. He said that when he signed the request he was aware that he would not be entitled to his full pension. Prior to signing it, he did not discuss it with the minister, nobody, neither the minister, Lukic, or anyone told him that he was going to be pensioned off at a lower pension than he would have been entitled to. He did not inquire or protest the decision because as far as he was concerned the decision had already been made. That is his explanation as to how he left the force so quickly, and again that is a matter for you to consider whether or not you believe him. When it was put to him that he would have been entitled to appeal the decision had he not signed this request, he obfuscated first by saying he didn't know. He said he didn't know whether he could appeal. And when it was put to him that in many documents where he had transferred or removed senior police officers, including SUP chiefs, there was a paragraph at the end of these documents telling them that they had a right to appeal within a certain time and he had signed many of those documents. He eventually accepted that he was entitled to appeal. His attempts to explain how he ended his career and his flight, Your Honours, become an era in his testimony that the Prosecution submits you should review cautiously. It is a matter for you, but the evidence indicates clearly that he was not being sincere with the Court as to how his career was terminated. His claims that he fled his homeland, Serbia, because of his fears of arrest are not of any merit. Even he says that the charge or the charge that he heard was being investigated against him of abuse of office was spurious. It does not square up at all, Your Honours, that a man with his career would flee because he has heard of a spurious allegation made against him for a relatively minor charge. So it is a matter for you to consider, Your Honours, whether or not his flight at that time when the bodies were discovered and the investigation started, investigation which interestingly included, according to the testimony, investigators from this Tribunal. But Your Honours should consider whether his flight arose from his own knowledge of his guilty participation and whether or not there is any other reasonable alternative to that finding. Turn now to another aspect of the case, Your Honour, Racak and the evidence of K86, a police officer or former police officer who testified that on the onset of that operation on the 15th of January, 1999, Mr. Djordjevic was present with the SUP chief and the Urosevac police chief at the Stimlje police station. K86, a very important witness for the Prosecution, his evidence shows that Mr. Djordjevic continued to exercise oversight and command responsibilities over the police in their activities in Kosovo in 1999. I think it is as a result of this that the Defence has launched an attack on the credibility of K86, comes in various ways. They say at paragraph 86 that he was not aware of Marinkovic's presence on the 15th and had he been present there on the 15th he would have had to know that the Racak investigation started on that day and that Marinkovic was present. The Defence assertion seems to be or they seem to be saying now that K86 was not there on the 15th. They make a point, Your Honours, but there is no citation of the trial record for any of those propositions on which they made the point. It says in paragraph 86. At paragraph 87 the Defence purports to contradict K86's testimony that deputy commander Mitrovic was at the police station that day by claiming that he was on sick leave, that is, deputy commander Mitrovic was on sick leave and they cite to D138 in support of that assertion. I invite the Court to have a look at D138. It does not support in any way the Defence assertion that deputy commander Mitrovic was on sick leave that day. At paragraph 90 they also sought to attack his credibility because he had recently been treated for post-trauma stress syndrome. I would submit that that doesn't reflect on his credibility on the matters that he had to testify about here, and the Defence could not identify any contradiction or inconsistency nor offer to the Court any reason why he would be untruthful to this Court. Your Honour, he -- the defence is that Mr. Djordjevic arrived there on the 18th just that make sure that there was an investigation. K86 says he saw him there on the 15th and K86 could not be mistaken because it is not a matter of the date, 18th or 15th, it's a matter of the circumstances. K86 says he saw him there the day of the operation. He related the sequence of events and the circumstances in which he saw him there. So he could not be mistaken. On the day the operation started, he saw Mr. Djordjevic there. Your Honour, not only is K86's evidence to this Court internally consistent and seamless, but it is to some degree confirmed by P1555, which is the transcript of the testimony of the SUP chief Janicevic, who testified before the ICTY in the Milosevic case where he was cross-examined. He said that he, as the SUP chief in charge of the operation, was present there on the 15th and Mr. Djordjevic was there on the 15th as well. Your Honours, the Prosecution notes and accepts that this is hearsay evidence. Mr. Janicevic is not before the Court and this Defence has not had an opportunity to cross-examine him, and therefore that must diminish the value of P1555. In addition, this is a statement about the acts and conduct of the accused, and that as well would diminish the weight of it. However, it is submitted that it is entirely within the Trial Chamber's discretion to attribute to it whatever weight it thinks fit at this point in the case when the Chamber is evaluating all the evidence and doing so in light of all of the evidence, particularly of those persons who testified about this event. And while conceding and accepting that there are factors which diminish the value of P155 [sic], the Prosecution submits that the evidence of Janicevic, the SUP chief responsible for the action, albeit hearsay, can have some reliability and lends some support and corroboration to K86's evidence regarding the presence of Djordjevic at the Stimlje police station that morning. Mr. Djordjevic -- to move on. Mr. Djordjevic was the man in charge of the police in Serbia. Everybody knew that, everybody treated him that way. All the senior MUP generals, all the senior police generals, all the senior politicians, and that is why he was the policeman that featured in all the negotiations with internationals in respect to Kosovo and signed all of -- and signed many of these agreements, particularly the October Agreements in 1998. The fundamental purpose of the October Agreements was to maintain a cease-fire in Kosovo, and you have before the Court K -- I'm sorry, P836, an understanding between KDOM and the Ministry of the Interior signed by Mr. Byrnes, Mr. Djordjevic. Interestingly, if I could read from Mr. Djordjevic's testimony at 10118 of the transcript. He said: "Shaun only saw me on negotiations. It wasn't me who decided to participate in negotiations, no. It was the president of Serbia and the minister of interior who decided that. I had spent years and years in Kosovo and what Byrnes said was quite natural. I knew every village, every hamlet, every path, every road, and I knew the circumstances there. But far be it that I was the supreme decision-maker there." Of course the Prosecution does not, does not, suggest that Djordjevic was at the head of the joint criminal enterprise. The allegations are that he, like Lukic, like other policemen - not all the policemen but some policemen, senior policemen, senior army commanders - participated. And the fact that Milosevic or Mr. Sainovic or Mr. Stojiljkovic were senior to him and perhaps were the leading figures and the original orders and plans emanated from them is not inconsistent with Mr. Djordjevic's guilt if he participated with awareness of what he was doing. But this quote from Mr. Djordjevic indicates that, as Mr. Byrnes said, he was very knowledgeable about Kosovo and he was in command. He's appointed by, no less, the president of the country and the minister. If we look to 837, P837, this is a record of a meeting in Belgrade of the same date, the 25th of October, 1998. In this agreement, again signed by Mr. Djordjevic and other very senior personnel, agreement was reached to scale-down the operations of police and VJ units in Kosovo. Djordjevic having signed both of these agreements would be aware of their requirements. If we look at page 2 and with -- you see: "With these goals in mind, the state authorities of the FRY have announced the following measures," and move on to page 3. And these are some of what is agreed. If you look at paragraph 3: "Police -- special police will resume their normal peace time activities. Heavy weapons and equipment remaining under MUP control in Kosovo will be returned to cantonments and police stations." So Mr. Djordjevic was aware of the requirements of these agreements, and he violated these agreements through his involvement in the Racak action. In that action the VJ and the MUP thwarted the very purpose of the agreements by attacking the KLA without informing the observers, and thereby they destroyed the fragile cease-fire and caused the cease-fire to collapse. According to Mr. Philipps, after that the regular meeting between the KVM and the liaison group stopped, and as Byrnes testified, at the end of the day Racak destroyed the October Agreements. One matter before I move on in respect to the agreements, and I don't wish to engage too much in any -- in submissions about the KLA. They, it is conceded, committed crimes themselves. But the Defence in their brief at paragraph 66 says: "As noted above, the purpose of the October Agreements was to verify the maintenance of cease-fire by all elements; however, the KLA was not a signatory to any of these agreements and the evidence shows that the suggestion that they become signatories was rejected by the KLA Main Staff. Their refusal to agree to a cease-fire and their action to the contrary are important factors in this intervening period." The evidence that the KLA's absence from the October negotiations was mainly because of the demands by the Serb and FRY officials. If we could look at P87. It's the record of a meeting on the 2nd of November, 1998, minutes of the meeting of the operations inter-departmental staff of the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija held at Beli Dvor palace in Belgrade on 29 October, chaired by President Milosevic, participating President Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Stojiljkovic, Mr. Andjelkovic Mr. Perisic, Mr. Pavkovic, Mr. Djordjevic, Mr. Stevanovic, Mr. Lukic. At page 2, General Pavkovic speaking on behalf of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija stated that just days after the signing of the October Agreements to participants -- may I re-read that. General Pavkovic said at page 2: "Efforts by foreign country to have the legitimacy of the so-called KLA as the armed force of the Siptar secessionist movement recognised by including the KLA in the solution of the Kosovo question was also very unfortunate for us." At page 13 of the same meeting or of the same document in respect to the same meeting, FRY President Slobodan Milosevic reminded the participants of the fact that influential international factors, especially German and the US, wanted to bring the so-called KLA into the position of a negotiator with the legal organs of our government, but the attempt was successful thwarted. So the proposition of the Defence at paragraph 66 of their brief does not square up with the record. Mr. Vasiljevic, General Vasiljevic, Your Honours, was another important witness in this case, an important witness for the Prosecution. He was a senior member of the VJ and he testified about Skorpions, paramilitaries in Kosovo, crimes that were committed, their incorporation into the MUP, the fact that it was well-known or could be easily discovered that the MUP was incorporating criminal elements. I won't go over that. That is well recited, I think, in the Prosecution's final brief. But he also testified about the 1st of June meeting, another very important meeting, the 1st of June meeting in Pristina, a meeting of the Joint Command that was attended by Mr. Djordjevic. This -- the Defence claims that Mr. Djordjevic -- Mr. Vasiljevic is either mistaken or not being honest when he says that Mr. Djordjevic attended this meeting. We see no motive presented as to why Mr. Vasiljevic would make something like this up, and he was cross-examined in quite significant detail about his evidence that Mr. Djordjevic was present at this meeting and responded carefully, ably, and convincingly, it is submitted. He could remember Mr. Djordjevic's presence at that meeting because Djordjevic was well-known within Serbia as the head of the police, and this was the first time they had met. So it was remembered before him that he was meeting this well-known figure. He recalled that they met later on at a meeting in July 1997, but this was the first time they met and it was therefore memorable to him. In fact, he remembered a specific comment Mr. Djordjevic made and if we could move to private session just for one moment, Your Honours, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, what that general would be doing in the field would be something that would be known to General Djordjevic, and it is reasonable and consistent that General Djordjevic would make that comment in respect to Mr. -- to that general's absence. Mr. Djordjevic was coming from the seat of the MUP in Belgrade and so was that general that he spoke of, they were coming from the same place, and he would know where that general was. The Defence called Mr. Stojanovic, General Stojanovic, who at the relevant time I think was a lieutenant-colonel and the chief of the security section in the command of the Pristina Corps, to say that Mr. Djordjevic was not present at that meeting on the 1st of July. And I ask Your Honours to reflect carefully on the evidence of Mr. Stojanovic. He was generally an incredible witness who tailored his evidence specifically to refute the testimony of his subordinate Nike Peraj who testified about various crimes that were committed in Meja. And he tailored his testimony specifically to refute the testimony of his superior, General Vasiljevic, but he's incredible primarily because of his absurd denial of any VJ wrong-doing. Most noticeably, Your Honours, he denied knowledge of the expulsions and murders that happened during the joint police/VJ operation at Meja. He's an intelligence -- the chief intelligence gatherer, the chief of security section for the Pristina command, and he would have the Court believe that he was not aware of this type of information. Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that when all the evidence is weighed together, General Vasiljevic's evidence is acceptable and reliable and the Court can act on it safely. If I move on quickly to the alternative mode of liability under Rule 7(3). The Prosecution's case is based primarily on evidence of the accused's knowing participation or contribution to the joint criminal enterprise and aiding and abetting and planning the crimes under Rule 7(1). However, the same evidence supports convictions under Rule 7(3) mode of liability. In fact, Your Honours might well think that this is the least troubling part of the case as evidence in respect to his responsibility or his individual criminal liability under Rule 7(3) is quite clear and straightforward. Most of it is beyond dispute; the remainder of it has been admitted by the accused. I won't go through the evidence in detail. That again has been set out in our pre-trial brief [sic], but we'll submit very quickly that the evidence establishes that Mr. Djordjevic's liable as a superior under Rule 7(3) for all the crimes charged in the indictment that were committed by members of the RJB because the elements required for his liability under Article 7(3) are fulfilled, primarily the subject of admissions. There was a superior -- one, there was a superior -- Your Honours, so far -- may I just say this before I continue. So far I have said "pre-trial brief" many times and I meant final trial brief. At all times I mean the final trial brief and not the pre-trial brief. The first element for 7(3) liability is that there was a superior/subordinate relationship between Djordjevic and the persons who committed the underlying crimes in the sense for Rule 7(3) that Djordjevic had a material ability to prevent and punish members of the RJB. Secondly, he knew or he had reason to know that the underlying crimes were about to be, were being, or had been committed and he failed to take -- certainly he failed to take the reasonable and necessary measures to prevent his subordinates from committing the underlying crimes or to punish them subsequent to their commission. It is submitted that the Podujevo incident is an unambiguous example of Mr. Djordjevic's individual criminal liability for murder under Rule -- or under Article 7(3). The perpetrators of the murders, members of the Skorpion unit, were incorporated into the public service -- public security sector as reserve policemen and were, therefore, his subordinates in the sense that he had the material ability to punish them at the minimum to cause and ensure that effective investigations were committed -- were commenced to inquire into allegations that they had committed crimes. At his level that is a minimum that would be expected of him and that is his material ability to punish under the law. Now, before I move on there is -- there was in the course of the case some dispute as to whether or not the Skorpions had been incorporated into the SAJ. I think it is beyond dispute that they were incorporated into the police as MUP reservists, but Mr. Stalevic and Mr. Simovic and even the accused seem to be suggesting that at the time of the Podujevo massacre they were not under the command of the SAJ, the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit. However, we see now that the Defence in its final trial brief has stated and seems to concede or accept now on review of the evidence that the reservists were attached to the SAJ, indicating that the Skorpions were under the SAJ command. This is at Defence final trial brief paragraphs 479, 480, 481, 483, 484, 488, 496, 509, and 511. It probably does not matter that much because if there were reservists in the police force it does not really matter if they had been attached to the SAJ at the time of the massacre. They were still within the ambit of his material ability to effect investigations, to punish. So these reservists, the Skorpions, committed this crime and the second element is notice. In this case he received from Mr. Simovic actual notice that some of these men had murdered civilians, including women and children. He admits that. There is no issue on the second element of actual notice. Thirdly, he failed to adopt any measures, any measures at all available to him to ensure that his subordinates, particularly Mr. Simovic, take any steps at all to investigate the incident and to identify the perpetrators. On the contrary, he acceded to Mr. Simovic sending away the perpetrators from the scene without any investigation; and worse, later he ordered Mr. Trajkovic to disband and disperse them without ensuring that investigations had been conducted to identify the perpetrators of this horrible massacre. He admitted these things, that he did all of these things, he took no steps in respect to the investigations and he accepted their removal from the scene without investigations and their dispersal without any inquiries being made. He says his failure is because it had been report to him and it was his belief on the evening of the 28th when he spoke to Mr. Simovic that the OUP of Podujevo had been informed and that the OUP would conduct an investigation, and that is why he did nothing. But, Your Honour, his failure to do anything becomes even more egregious when we see the reports that he was receiving the next day. If we could look at D296. D296 is a MUP staff daily report for Kosovo on the 29th of March, and you see here it covers a period 0600 hours on the 28th of March -- sorry, 28th of March, 1999, 0600 hours, to the 29th of March, the period of the massacre. Paragraph 5 is for serious crimes committed. And if you look through it, Your Honours, you will see at paragraph 5 for serious crimes committed nothing. Your Honours, I ask you to assess the accused as a reasonable police officer, as a man endowed with all the attributes that we know about Mr. Djordjevic as chief of the police. His subordinates or he's told that his subordinates lined up 20-odd women and children and shot them, killing I think it was 16. Some lived to come and testify. He doesn't do anything about it because it's supposed to be investigated. The very next day it comes on his desk, the report, from the people who are supposed to be investigating it and they say there is no serious crime. What would any reasonable police chief do? What is his duty under Article 7(3)? His excuse for doing nothing is that he thought something was being done on the 28th. Now he knows, now he receives indications at least that nothing is being done. Your Honours should review the record of his testimony when he was asked about this. He could not explain why he did nothing, having received it, having been advised that nothing was being done. He merely just insisted that he was told previously that the OUP would be brought in. Your Honours, it is noteworthy that no investigations at all were conducted under the -- of this horrendous crime, and although there is evidence that the investigating judge was brought to the scene, the evidence is that they were brought to the scene three days later. According to Mr. Vasiljevic they were brought there three days later and they presented a -- they did an on-site report three days later of I think about two pages in respect to this crime. Disciplinary proceedings or investigations for disciplinary purposes within the police force would not have been sufficient for mass murder, but Djordjevic also had a duty to do internal disciplinary investigations, if only, if only, to identify who were the perpetrators and end their career in the force or stop them at least from carrying weapons until they were charged criminally. The Prosecution submits that Mr. Djordjevic had two responsibilities, to ensure that his subordinates on the ground took all the steps necessary of collecting evidence, interviewing people, and bringing -- and starting or initiating a criminal investigation. He did not do that. And he also had a responsibility to take internal disciplinary investigative steps to identify the perpetrators and at least relieve them of duty until they were charged. As it turned out, because he did nothing, many of these shooters who murdered these women and children returned to Kosovo in April when Mr. Djordjevic authorised that the Skorpions be regrouped and sent back. They returned to Kosovo under the auspices of the police because of his failure. These failures, Your Honour, or these elements in respect to 7(3), Article 7(3) liability for Podujevo are all admitted. Before we look at the requirements of the law enforcement agencies, I should point out that the Defence trial brief at 693, paragraph 693 and elsewhere, claims that Mr. Djordjevic would not know of the crimes that were being committed in Kosovo because the daily reports that were coming up from the MUP staff and the SUPs did not include these crimes. And we see one, and this is a very interesting document, very interesting document, D296, because it shows clearly that Mr. Djordjevic must have known of the policy of his senior policemen in Kosovo covering up crimes, covering up massacres against civilians. He knew on the 28th that a score of women and children were lined up and shot by his subordinates. The next day his senior subordinate in Kosovo does not report that this crime occurred. I asked him: Well, what did he do about it? Nothing. Did he call up the SUP chief, MUP staff chief, and say what is a serious crime in your books? No. Why? His answer was: Well, I heard that the thing was being investigated. Your Honours, that was not the point. The point is: What does he do when he realises that his subordinates are not reporting serious crimes? Nothing. The Court is entitled to find that he was aware of the policy of covering up serious crimes and he did nothing because he agreed with it and he facilitated it as the head of the service. If we could look quickly at D855, this is a long criminal procedure of the former SFRY, but it was operational in Serbia at the relevant time according to Judge Marinkovic. Go quickly to Article 151, 1-5-1: "If there are grounds to suspect that a crime which is automatically prosecuted has been committed, law enforcement agencies must take the steps necessary to locate the perpetrator of the crime, to prevent the perpetrator or accomplice from hiding or fleeing, to detect and preserve the clues to the crime and articles which might serve as evidence and to gather all information which might be of use to effective conduct of criminal proceedings. "... law enforcement agencies must take the necessary information from individual citizens ..." Your Honours, I ask you -- I will not read it all, but these reflect the usual responsibilities of policemen on the ground, although an investigating judge should turn up to take charge of the investigations, policemen on the ground have a responsibility to inquire, apprehend, collect evidence until the investigating judge is arriving. If we could look at Article 152, paragraph (1), I ask the Court to review these laws more carefully when time permits: "Authorised officers of law enforcement agencies have the right to send persons found at the scene of the crime to the examining magistrate or to detain them until he arrives if such persons might provide information important to the criminal proceedings and if it is probable that they could not be interrogated at a subsequent date ..." If we look at 154, paragraph (2): "If the examining magistrate is unable to come to the scene immediately, law enforcement agencies may themselves conduct an inquest on the spot and order the necessary expert evaluations, except autopsy and exhumation of a corpse. If the examining magistrate reaches the scene during an inquest he may undertake to perform these actions. The public prosecutor shall be informed about everything done." Your Honours, Mr. Simovic was told that the Skorpions committed a crime, sent away the men, didn't detain them, he didn't wait for the investigating magistrate to come, he didn't collect any evidence. The investigating magistrate did not arrive until three days later when some of the bodies were still there, three days. In that period of time the police had responsibilities. The police did nothing, and the steps taken by the MUP after this incident were manifestly inadequate and Mr. Djordjevic must have known they were manifestly inadequate. If we look quickly at P1591, page 4, it's a record of Mr. Simovic's interview at the Prokuplje trial in 2001 or 2002. Said: "For the third or fourth time now, the Court insists that I give my final opinion about who, or whose member, fired at the civilians." It is clear, Your Honours, that those Judges were shocked and outraged by Mr. Simovic's inaction, his failure to do what was his responsibility to do. Mr. Simovic reported his inaction to Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Djordjevic did not express the same outrage and did not do his duty to ensure that his commanders on the ground investigated this crime. Your Honours, I ask you to review even the concern and the questions by this Chamber to Mr. Simovic when he testified from 13623 to 1327 -- 13627 of the transcript. It was manifest, manifest, that Simovic, having been in charge of these men, leaving -- he left the same day and hightailed it to Belgrade without knowing if any OUP had come on the scene, any investigating judge. He sent away the men, and that is what he told Mr. Djordjevic; Mr. Djordjevic did nothing. I won't bother to go over the question and the answers put to Mr. Simovic by this Court, also clearly outraged by his inaction. It seemed, Your Honours, that the only person who was not outraged by the inaction of the police to investigate this was the commander, Mr. Djordjevic. On the issue of 7(3), these admissions by the accused, entitles the Judge -- the Chamber to find that all of the elements have been satisfied and to find him guilty under 7(3), Article 7(3) for this murder. The Prosecution further submits that in light of Mr. Djordjevic's own evidential guard against participation in the concealment of the bodies, he is also liable under Article 7(3) for each and all of the incidents of murder specifically enumerated in paragraph 75 of the indictment. The evidence proving the required elements for conviction under 7(3) are again not susceptible to reasonable dispute being mostly admitted by the accused. The evidence in respect to several murder sites specifically referred to in the indictment, Suva Reka, Podujevo, Bela Crkva, Mala Krusa, Milos Gilic Street, Pusto Selo, and Suceska is that the perpetrators of these massacres included policemen who were Djordjevic's subordinates under Rule 7(3) -- Article 7(3).
