This is -- and when I say subordinates under Article 7(3), I make a distinction between whether or not he was in Kosovo because he says that he was not in Kosovo and he was not commanding them in the operations, but for purposes of Article 7(3) they are subordinates if he had a material ability to punish them, and at his level his material ability would be to ensure that disciplinary and criminal proceedings are commenced against them and he had that power. That is not disputed. He admitted in his evidence, Your Honours, the second element, that at the time when he participated in the concealment of the human bodies he was aware that these bodies or these were the bodies of victims of crimes and he accepted in his evidence that he was aware of the possibility that the perpetrators were police officers. This is at 10011 of the record. That, according to the jurisprudence and Article 7(3), is sufficient notice, inquiry notice. The difference in Podujevo, with regard to Podujevo, he was told specifically about that crime, he had specific notice. Here he had inquiry notice, this is ought-to-know section. He was put on inquiry, he accepts that. A superior will be deemed to have reason to know when he's possessed of information sufficiently alarming to justify inquiry. I submit to the Court that 800 dead bodies being concealed is sufficiently alarming to justify inquiry. The information may be general in nature and does not need to include specific details about unlawful acts which have been committed, so he has admitted to that element. He has admitted to the third element in respect to these murders, Your Honours, because he said that he knew that it was his duty to properly investigate these killings, that he should have acted accordingly; and he admitted to this Court that he failed to do so. In this context he said in cross-examination, and I quote: "I acted the way I did at the moment. I accepted his," that's the minister's, "orders without opposing him. I'm aware that this was a big mistake I made but what happened cannot be made undone. I'm ashamed of my deeds and I believe that the Court's decision will be adequate and I will be held responsible for what I did." Transcript 10006. He has admitted all the elements, all the formal elements required for conviction under Rule 7(3) -- Article 7(3) for murder in respect to all of the scheduled murder incidents in the indictment. Your Honours, the Prosecution further submits that in respect to all the other incidents of murder involving perpetrators from the public service department and having regard to the admissions made, Mr. Djordjevic knew or ought to have known that murders of Kosovo Albanians were being committed by his subordinates in Kosovo and that, as he put it, to quote him: "The situation required a full check and that all the facts needed to be established." And that: "A commission or a group ought to have been set up to investigate it." This is transcript 9723 to 4 and transcript 10002. Again, the Court is entitled to act on the admissions that he has made before you. Your Honours, I move on to a variety of issues, matters in the Defence brief which at the beginning I indicated I wanted to meet, because it is the position of the Prosecution that many of these propositions are erroneous, not based on the evidence or mis-characterise the evidence. And I wish to begin by making a correction to the Prosecution's final trial brief. At page 304, paragraph 1232, footnote 3336, the reference to K84 should be removed and the correct citation should be Djordjevic at transcript 9973 to 9975, Exhibit P1508, P815, pages 31 to 35. Another correction is at paragraph 567 of the Prosecution's closing brief, third sentence, 35 -- it is -- I'll read the third sentence. "35 to 37 corpses were later exhumed and identified as having originated from Kosovo." This is in relation to the mass grave at Bajina Basta, Lake Perucac. And the footnote in respect to the sentence I just read was cited to Mr. Baraybar. That is not correct and that footnote should be removed. The proper footnote or the proper reference is K84 at transcript 2043 to 2046 and transcript 2075, both in closed session; and also P394. And to just explain that a little bit further, K84 was investigating these mass graves in Serbia gave an estimate of 37 corpses found at Bajina Basta at the site of Lake Perucac. However, Your Honours would be aware that the forensic anthropologist who actually did the excavation and disinterment of the bodies counted at least 48 bodies. And -- right. I'm corrected also. The proper citation, therefore, or the evidence in respect to the 48 individuals is Sterenberg P815, that's the excavation report at page 37, paragraph 1. The Defence claims, and I'll just run through some of these matters very quickly. The Defence claims at paragraph 586: "Not a single piece of evidence was presented during the trial that would in any way associate Mr. Djordjevic with the event at Petrovo Selo." That is the mass graves at Petrovo Selo. This is manifestly not the case, Your Honour. There is evidence that entitles the Court to infer that he was a party to the operations of burying bodies at the -- at Petrovo Selo. This is set out in the Prosecution's closing brief at paragraphs 303 to 305. There are several items there which makes it readily apparent that Petrovo Selo was part of the same operation as Batajnica. However, there's an additional point that was not addressed in the brief. The original refrigerator truck that was found floating in the Danube near Tekija was ordered destroyed by Mr. Djordjevic. The evidence of Mr. Radojkovic who destroyed it and also Mr. Golubovic is that the truck, the truck, from Batajnica was transferred to the MUP facility in Petrovo Selo and destroyed there. So that an additional piece of evidence showing that the Petrovo Selo burial operations is part of the same transaction as the Batajnica burial operations that the accused admitted to. The Defence argues at paragraphs 559 to 560 of its brief that there is no evidence that shows that the order to destroy the truck in which the bodies had been found -- I'll just read it. I'll quote it, Your Honours: "There is no evidence that shows that the order to destroy the truck in which the bodies had been found was a consequence of any direct order of Vlastimir Djordjevic." This is in paragraphs 559 to 560 of the brief. Your Honours, this is splitting hairs or even worse it's decimating hairs because the Defence admitted or Mr. Djordjevic admitted at transcript 9726, line 16, that on the minister's instructions he told Djordjevic to destroy the truck. So I don't know if the Defence is trying to say that it was not a direct order of Djordjevic simply because Mr. Djordjevic said that he convoyed the minister's instructions, but that is splitting hairs. Djordjevic ordered the destruction of the trucks by his own admission. And Mr. Golubovic in his testimony at 1715, that's 1715 and 1755 to 56, he said too that Djordjevic told him to have the refrigerator lorry destroyed, and so it was. Defence, if I could move on, argues for several paragraphs, 549 to 554 that the concealment operations in Tekija were not intentionally kept secret. They appeared to focus on the question of whether Mr. Djordjevic officially classified this as a state secret. There is no merit in this argument, Your Honours. Mr. Djordjevic himself testified at transcript 9721 that he instructed

utterances.speaker: MR. GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: "All further action in relation to this should be kept confidential so that the public was not informed." If I could move on, the Defence make the repeated assertion in their brief that Mr. Djordjevic intended to have the bodies autopsied at some point. They go so far as to suggest that the bodies -- that Mr. Djordjevic wanted the bodies to be autopsied in Tekija and that he intended the bodies at Batajnica to be autopsied eventually. This is obvious or this is opposite to the clear evidence that there was never any intention to autopsy or properly process these bodies. And I ask the Chamber to review the Chamber's own questioning of Mr. Golubovic in this regard at page 1746 of the reference. The transcript indicated that Presiding Judge Parker asked: "Well, what I'm not clear about then is why if you had no pathologist and no judge, either municipal or district, and no prosecutor, you would have thought of burying these bodies that night." And the answer: "Well, the reason was we had to move the refrigerator truck further off the road because the people who were near the refrigerator truck said that there was already a stench spreading of decomposing bodies. It just couldn't stay like that without being dealt with, so that was the reason for us trying to deal with this as quickly as possible." Effectively, avoidance or evasion of a direct question put to him by the Court, and it continues on and on in that reference in the transcript to questions being asked about this supposed intention to have these bodies autopsied. The claim that Mr. Djordjevic was interested in forensic examinations at a later time has no foundation on the evidence, completing lacking in merit. Mr. Djordjevic had no intention of doing so and he never did so, nor did he at any time when he had the opportunity up until 2007 and even beyond inform anyone of the location of these bodies. To the contrary, he took steps to maintain the cover-up until the bodies were discovered by others. I ask the Court to note that after the conflict in June 1997, Mr. Trajkovic, according to him in his evidence, expressed concern about the bodies being at his, that is, Mr. Trajkovic's, base. Mr. Trajkovic, if you recall, Your Honours, was head of the SAJ and Djordjevic's immediate subordinate. And Djordjevic spoke to Mr. Trajkovic and accepted the potential need to move the bodies away from Batajnica, that is, just to continue the cover-up. The Defence made allegations in respect to ethnicity. At paragraph 604, the Defence says in its brief that Mr. Djordjevic did not know about the ethnicity of the bodies. Your Honours, this does not square up with Mr. Golubovic's testimony or even Mr. Djordjevic's own testimony. Mr. Golubovic testified that he told Mr. Djordjevic that the victims were dressed in the fashion or the manner of Kosovar Albanians and the truck had markings of having come from Prizren. Mr. Djordjevic testified at 9730 of the transcript: "He(the minister) said that since I was already familiar with the matter and that I knew from our previous contacts that these were bodies which came from Kosovo and Metohija, in other words, that these were the bodies of Albanians, that it was necessary to bury them ..." So Mr. Djordjevic's evidence contradicts this proposition. In fact, at different parts of the Defence brief, the Defence seems to make the concession that Mr. Djordjevic knew where the bodies came from because the minister told him. So in the final trial brief -- in their final trial brief at paragraph 557, they state that having realised that General Djordjevic was resolved to have the matter investigated, the minister told him that he, himself, was behind the whole story, that there had been some incidents in KiM, that is, Kosovo and Metohija, and that something had to be done to conceal the bodies. So this is the Defence's own submission elsewhere in the brief, indicating that the -- that Mr. Djordjevic was aware of the ethnicity of the victims, that they came from Kosovo. And the Defence, when they made that submission, they cited to Djordjevic's testimony at 9723 to 4 and what he actually said at 9723, line 24, and thereafter: "Only after he had realised," that's he, the minister, "had realised that I was commited to taking steps in order to clarify the whole matter, me made it known to me that he was fully behind. That certain incidents had happened down there and that something should be done in order to prevent the revelation of the finding of these bodies because of the whole NATO campaign and bombing." So the Defence is conceding that when Mr. Djordjevic said that the minister referred to these bodies having come from "down there," Mr. Djordjevic was, in fact, actually referring to down there in Kosovo and Metohija. Respectfully, Your Honours, it is submitted that there is no real doubt or issue that Mr. Djordjevic was aware that these bodies were of Kosovar Albanians. The Defence in its final trial brief argues in respect to the Skorpions that final -- that -- sorry, that background checks were properly conducted. That's paragraph 480. MUP police administration performed background checks of the men based on SUP records. Firstly, the Defence makes its claim without citing any evidence in support of this claim, and the Prosecution submits that there were no background checks on these men. The Skorpions contain men who had criminal records, their general reputation was of a criminal type, and I'm quoting General Vasiljevic at 5662 of the record: "Their general reputation was of criminal types in their ranks, problematic people, people with criminal records." The Skorpions were not even trained. Stoparic testified that he had to give them a crash course in using weapons or some of them a crash course in using weapons, and according to Witness K92 who was involved in or gathering together these Skorpions, Mr. Djordjevic did not inquire about whether or not they had received any training. He just accepted them. So that submission by the Defence that these men -- that there were in fact proper checks made is not supported, they haven't cited anything to support it, and the evidence is to the contrary. Indeed, no one involved in the recruitment or command of this body of men was able to say that they had in fact been checked and screened. They merely said that they were supposed to be, police administration was supposed to do this, but nobody said anything that supports the Defence submissions. Identification and I give -- before I move on, I gave a reference to Mr. Vasiljevic just now in terms of what he said about the fact that these Skorpions contained persons' criminal records. The proper citation, it's transcript 5667. Defence in its final trial brief, at paragraph 485, argues that the perpetrators of the Podujevo massacre could not be identified at the crime scene. The references usually given in support of this proposition do not support it and this is mere argumentation. As a matter of fact, the evidence in respect to Podujevo is quite clear, nothing was gone, so it cannot be argued that the perpetrators of the massacre could not be identified. However, we should recall the evidence of Mr. Stoparic that some of the Skorpions who objected tried -- these are the foot soldiers, some of the men on the ground who participated in this sort of thing, they, themselves, tried to do an inquiry themselves. Who were the ones who participated in it? And that inquiry was stopped and there was no follow-up. So the assertion by the Defence that they could not be identified has no merit, particularly because no efforts were made to identify them as was the requirement of the law. There is a lot of submissions in respect of the Skorpions about Trajkovic being effectively responsible for the reservists. Many of these submissions the Court will, no doubt, look at the references and assess them for what they are, but the Prosecution does not deny, even though the Defence in its -- in making many of their references, are quite wrong. But Trajkovic was the commander of the reservists and was responsible for their actions. We accept that, but Trajkovic himself said that he reported to Mr. -- he was the direct subordinate of Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Vasiljevic's evidence in regard to the paramilitaries generally and the Skorpions in particular is of significant importance in this case, especially when the Court considers questions as to why men of this quality should be incorporated into a police force. And so, of course, the Defence sought to attack his evidence, one means being at paragraph 506 where they say that his evidence in regard to the information that he got on the paramilitaries operating in Kosovo was preliminary and unconfirmed. They say that Mr. -- or they tried to impugn his credibility when they say that he denied the facts contained in D210, a report of the security administration of the Supreme Command Staff. Well, he did deny or did not -- or refused to accept the facts in that document, but this does not make him an unreliable witness. In fact, it demonstrates that the report itself was unreliable and its authenticity questionable. If we review the record at transcript 5913, we'll see it clear from the intervention of the Presiding Judge that the doubts about the authenticity of D210 was clearly raised by the witness. The Prosecution submits that Mr. -- General Vasiljevic's credibility could not be rationally impugned on the basis of his refusal to accept that document. Various other claims are made about Mr. Vasiljevic, one of them, the last one which I'll address, is the claim made by the Defence that all - and they say all - the evidence provided by Mr. Vasiljevic concerning crimes and paramilitary units was preliminary and unconfirmed. And the reference that the Defence makes in its trial brief is to transcript 5897, and that does not support the Defence assertion that Mr. Vasiljevic's information was unconfirmed. As a matter of fact, Your Honours, Mr. Vasiljevic actually rejected the Defence proposition that these were preliminary reports and said that the reports and information he received was not initial information and what -- and he received reports in great detail about the operations of these paramilitary units, which is a natural thing. He's a chief or the deputy chief of the security administration in the VJ. They are in operations. He would be expected to know in detail about the movements and the operations of other armed paramilitary groups in the area where the VJ was. So even in terms of logic, in addition to the evidence, General Djordjevic -- General Vasiljevic's evidence is reliable and credible, it is submitted. The Defence at paragraphs 512 to 514 seem to argue that there were no paramilitary units in Kosovo during the war. This is probably a misunderstanding because that is completely and wholly contrary to the evidence. I won't deal with that any further. The Defence argues in its closing brief at paragraphs 605 to 608 that the arming of civilians was done in an undiscriminatory way in compliance with the Law on Defence. The Prosecution submits that this was not unmeritorious. The arming was done along ethnic lines. During 1998 and 1999 the MUP and VJ covertly armed over 600.000 [sic] non-Albanian citizens from local villages and towns, and they referred to, quite specifically, many of the documents referred to them as non-Siptar population. And without further ado, I would just submit that this is -- -- and the number is 60.000, not 600.000. 60.000 men, civilians, sorry, were armed and these were of Serbian ethnicity. This would be a very, very high proportion of the Serbian population in Kosovo. And Mr. Cvetic, SUP chief at 6719 and Mr. Djakovic, VJ general at 8139, confirmed that the ethnic Albanians were excluded from these RPOs. Defence argument, again at paragraph 609 of the brief, is that there is no evidence whatever that Mr. Djordjevic had any knowledge or that he received any information about the engagement of the armed and non-Albanian population in 1999. They say that there is no evidence whatever that he knew about these armed persons. I submit, Your Honours, that he clearly knew about the policy in 1999 and of the plans to use them. I'd ask the Court to look briefly at P85. I used the document earlier. It's one of the important documents of the case. This is the 17th of February meeting, 17th of February, 1999, meeting, at the stage where operations that would lead to all of these murders and all of these expulsions were planned and being discussed. Mr. Lukic reported in Mr. Djordjevic's presence that RPOs in nearly all villages inhabited by Serbs: "RPOs in all villages inhabited by Serbs are very active. Meetings have been held with all the RPOs and they were attended by General Stojanovic and Lieutenant-Colonel Blagoje Pesic. Their work and engagement have been assessed as good."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll adjourn and resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Moving on to the defence's submission in respect to the Joint Command at paragraphs 298 and 299 and elsewhere in the brief, they assert that the Joint Command was just a series of information sharing meetings that no orders could be given at Joint Command meetings and that it did not continue to exist after October 1998. The Defence's position is fundamentally inconsistent with the extent of evidence detailing the Joint Command's existence and actions in both 1998 and 1999, and this is addressed at length by the Prosecution in its brief at paragraphs 267 to 311. And one specific allegation of the Defence that there were different participation -- because there were different participants at each meeting indicates that there were people simply exchanging information from the ground. This is at paragraph 299 of the brief. Ignores the fact that it is easily discernible from the Joint Command minutes that there were core members that attended most meetings or virtually every meeting to the point that if one of them did not attend the absence would be specifically recorded in the minutes. So the fact that other persons participated does not negate the fact that this was a command structure. The Defence argues that - and this is in paragraph 22 of its brief - that the Joint Command is left as the only source of action of the alleged joint criminal enterprise. This is elaborated upon further in paragraph 297 of the brief where they say that by abandoning the theory of the Supreme Defence Council commanding all forces in executing the alleged plan, this modification leaves the so-called Joint Command as a main source of charged plurality of an alleged joint criminal enterprise. This is not correct. And I invite the Court to refer to paragraphs 20 to 25 of the indictment, particularly paragraph 20, which sets out the leading members of the JCE. The Supreme Defence Council and the Joint Command are two of the organisations, two of the instruments or command structures that were used to effect the JCE, but the plurality, if one can call it that, or the membership of the JCE is set out in paragraph 20 of the indictment. And the members of the Joint Command use several command bodies as instruments to effect the JCE. Now in this trial some of these command bodies are more or less relevant to the liability of the accused. The SDC which we haven't led much evidence on is more relevant to the liability of political accused and the chief of the VJ who are not before the Court. But the Prosecution does not abandon any theory in respect to the SDC. In respect to the crime base evidence, the Defence at paragraph 686 seems to challenge the evidence of [indiscernible], the UNHCR regarding the number of refugees and the fact that he said the vast majority of the refugees were Albanians. They say that his numbers are confusing because in his final summary, P734, he refers to 896.000 refugees and that does not match up with the cumulative estimate of 780.000 refugees of 10 June 1999. The Prosecution does not dispute that this -- there is a difference here, but there can be no real dispute that approximately 800.000 Albanians left Kosovo from the 24th of March to the 10th of June, 1999. In addition to the UNHCR's number, the MUP's own reporting shows similar numbers and also shows that the refugees were Albanian. On the 1st of May, 1999, over a month before the end of the NATO intervention, it was reported in P694, and is a MUP report, that 715.158 persons "belonging to the Siptar national minority" had left the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. And this is the figure to the end of April 1999. So the figures are more or less consistent between the UNHCR and the Defence document and the Defence document also accepts that these were Kosovo Albanians. The Defence generally in respect to the crime base, they argue many places in their brief but primarily from paragraphs 669 and thereafter that the crime base witnesses could not identify the perpetrators of the crime against them. Specifically we had translation difficulties in court where the witnesses identified colours. Some witnesses said they saw "milicija" on police uniforms, but "milicija" was no longer on uniforms. Many witnesses describe the forces as wearing green; however, this isn't sufficient because some KLA units wore green. Many people described the MUP as wearing ribbons, but the MUP changed the ribbon colours according to the schedule each day, and some witnesses' description of the ribbons did not correspond with the schedule. It is submitted, Your Honours, that there can be no serious question that the crime-base witnesses knew the Serb forces; namely, the VJ soldier, the MUP policemen, the paramilitaries, and the armed Serb civilians, they knew about the crimes that were being committed against them. There is a difference, Your Honour. It might well be said that a witness might not be able to identify an individual because of the circumstances in which an event occurred, but this is not a matter of identifying an individual. It's identifying a group of persons and it is submitted that it is not a sequence -- a commendable or a meritorious submission to say that Kosovar Albanians could not tell the difference between police and soldiers and could not tell the difference between police and armed Serb civilians. These crimes, Your Honours, were committed in broad daylight, most of them, and the civilian witnesses were in the presence of these perpetrators for significant periods of time before they were expelled from their homes. So it is submitted that these Kosovar Albanians would have seen policemen in their municipalities and villages and knew what policemen looked like, knew what they wore. And we have detailed -- in our closing brief, in respect to each individual crime site, the documentary evidence, much of these from the VJ, that corroborates these witnesses showing that VJ and MUP forces were indeed deployed and present in these areas conducting operations at the relevant time. And again, Your Honours, it is submitted that it is a non-commendable argument to suggest that Kosovar Albanians civilians in being expelled from their homes would not know the difference between the KLA and a Serb soldier or policeman. The Defence at paragraph 708, paragraph 70 -- well, 720 made the general argument that people left because of fear of NATO bombing. People left because of fighting between the force and the KLA, but not because of the acts of the Serb forces. Without going into the evidence, the submission very quickly is that the witnesses consistently referring to themselves and a whole class of people, their villages, everybody were leaving, they were consistent in saying that they left because they were forced out, they were expelled and they feared for their lives because they were aware of persons being murdered and otherwise abused. These witnesses were from different parts of Kosovo, they had different backgrounds, and in most cases they didn't know each other. The only thing in common, Your Honour, was their expulsion, the confiscation of their ID cards, and other indicia which we have discussed in the final trial brief in the section on the patterns of the crime. In their final trial brief, Your Honour, the Defence addressed each crime site in turn, and in the section the Prosecution has noted that in some circumstances they misstate or mis-characterise the evidence of the witness and they often make claims without any supporting evidence. It is not possible at this stage to go through all of them. I just ask the Court to exercise caution in -- as I believe the Court will in reviewing the evidence which is referred to. I have some examples to highlight which are not exhaustive, and even of these examples I will not go through all of them. For example, in respect to Pristina, the Defence brief states at paragraph 817 that K14 only left Kolevice having been forced to do so by unidentified persons, that is, after her brother spoke to unidentified men at the door of the place in which they lived. They decided it was dangerous for them to stay. That is not a proper characterisation of the evidence. She said uniformed policemen and soldiers came to their home and told them to leave, and they did as they were told. This is at 8993 of her transcript and P1325, which is her statement. The Defence in respect to Pristina and in respect to Bala, the witness Bala, they state in paragraph 813 that the identifications of Bala and her family were not taken at any point in time. And the purpose of this submission is to dilute the evidence in respect to the confiscation of IDs, and it is misleading because Bala directly observed Serb forces taking and destroying Albanians' identification. They were asked, it was Bala's testimony, and this is in P41 of her statement and at transcript T2344, they were asked for their IDs, but they did not have them and they told that to the Serb forces. And because there were hundreds or thousands of people, the Serb forces did not continue or force them to give up their IDs. If I may re-read this. Because there were so many people there, the Serb forces did not continue asking for everyone's IDs. In respect to Suva Reka -- and I indicate to the Court that this is not even close to the amount of mis-characterisations the Prosecution submits exist, but I just move on quickly to Suva Reka, which is the place of the Berisha family massacre. At paragraph 770 the Defence says, if I may -- I'll move on from this one because I cannot find the correct cite, but I think the Defence in respect to Podujevo -- in respect to Suva Reka, yes, the second paragraph -- the second sentence of the paragraph of 770 the Defence said: "According to 62, the whole town, the whole town of Suva Reka was in the hands of the KLA ." They don't cite to where and when 62 is supposed to have said this. No citation of the record is made. And this is contrary to the evidence of Hysni Berisha, Halit Berisha, K83, Shyhrete Berisha, who were living in the town at the time. K83 was, in fact, a policeman who witnessed a murder at Suva Reka. So this is an unsupported statement about what was happening in Suva Reka. The KLA were not operating there. There was some KLA presence 2 or 3 kilometres away from Suva Reka town; namely, on the right side of the road to Prizren in the village of Dobrodeljane and Semetiste and on the road to Restane about 2 kilometres from the town. So that statement is not correct, and in any case it would not -- well, it boggles the mind to see how that would explain the massacre. Paragraph 773, the submission is that the Suva Reka incident was an incident in fact involving individuals acting for personal reasons. Well, this is an argument that the Prosecution submits that this defies logic, that this killing could be simply personal reasons. Having regard to the number of policemen present and participating in the event in the middle of the town that day, it's clear that the Berisha murders were preplanned. The evidence of the police K83 directly indicates that when he arrived back at the police station he was sent off to join the others or other policemen who were committing the murders. And shortly after the massacre occurred, the mayor of the town Boban Vuksanevic [phoen], arrived with a truck to remove the bodies and this indicates that they must have known about or known in advance about the massacre. And we also have the policeman Velickovic whose evidence was that after the killings there was an order that came down from Belgrade to stop it, the killings should stop it, and they should just expel the Kosovar Albanians. The Defence argument in respect to Milos Gilic, this is not a mis-characterisation; it's an argument which we submit lacks logic. They argue at 841 that Dren Caka, being only 10 year's time, was not able to identify the forces, could not say -- or the Court should not accept his testimony in respect to who committed the massacre. He, Your Honour, if you review his testimony and I respectfully ask that you do so, he could describe the uniforms or the police who came to Vesa's house on the night of the 1st of April. He could describe -- he could identify the uniforms on the Exhibit 1301 which was a photo-board of police uniforms with police uniforms and other uniforms. And he identified photos 913, 14, and other photos, quite properly police uniforms. And when the Defence showed him different patterns of uniforms, he could identify, and this is D360, they showed him that and he could identify the blue uniforms worn by the police. And he has been consistent. We -- he was young at the time, but this was a situation where he was with his family and there is no issue that he could not see who the perpetrators were and -- in that town where he lived did not know policemen and could not, as a class as a group of people, tell who policemen were. Even if he could not see or identify an individual, but he would know who policemen were. And he has been very consistent in his testimony as to who the perpetrators were in both testimonies -- in previous testimonies and also in the video that was filmed when he was in a field hospital in April 1999 in Albania just days after the massacre. That's P1302 which was shown in the course of the evidence. In respect to Djakovica, the Defence claims that at paragraph 813 that Lizane Malaj who was also in Korenica testified that those in mixed uniforms told them to go to Albania; however, the next day Aco Mucinovic [phoen], an officer of the MUP, returned the civilians to their village. This shows that there was no plan to deport or forcibly transfer and certainly none involving the MUP. This is, it is submitted, misleading. If one reviews her evidence at transcript 809 to 818 and 830 to 832 and 865, her evidence was that on the 4th of April the police expelled her, her family, and other families from Korenica and they all left in a convoy. She agreed, accepted, that they were later ordered back to Korenica. But the Defence ignores her testimony that on the 27th of April about 35 men, some wearing blue camouflage, others wearing green camouflage, and others wearing mask, entered her courtyard, robbed the people, separated out the men, and ordered her and the rest of her family to walk to Albania. Some of these men were shot and their bodies later found at a police base in Batajnica later on. And the fact that the bodies, Your Honours, are found at a police base and part of this police cover-up, indicates that it was policemen who did the shooting of these men. So that is to clarify the -- what is said about her evidence. And if I may just make one quick point here in this regard. The Prosecution does not say that every senior policeman or police or soldier in Kosovo was a participant. So the fact that somebody might have assisted some of these refugees. For example, Nike Peraj, one of the Prosecution witnesses, a soldier testified that when he went up the valley there were so many killings going on that he was able, along with some other police officers, to stop some of the murders. So we don't say that it is impossible that on occasions some police officers and some members of the army were repelled by what was happening and acted to stop it when they could. So the fact that they were sent home at one point in time does not negate the evidence in support of a plan. And the Defence states that at 753 in respect to Prizren, that Latifi's testimony shows that he voluntarily left for Albania and was not deported or forcibly transferred. Further, his documents were not taken at any point. Your Honours, Latifi clearly said that the chief of police of Prizren ordered all the local residents to leave and go to Albania. He clearly states that the people were expelled and this is in his statement page 38 and it's P779. He also said -- statement that at the border crossing their documents were taken away. What he said is that he managed to hide his driver's licence, but all the other documents were taken away. So they -- the evidence is completely contrary to the submission that he left voluntarily. Defence makes claims in respect to Witness Krasniqi in respect to the same site, Prizren, that his documents were not confiscated, and this is at paragraph 755 of their brief. He did say, Your Honours, that he did not personally give up his documents, but his evidence was that at the check-points along the way to the Albanian border the police were confiscating the documents of many people. So his evidence should be looked at in that context. Your Honours, I have come to the end of the submissions I have to make. As I indicated, there are materials that the Prosecution could address you on further; however, the Prosecution believes that the Court is fully seized of this matter and is satisfied in leaving the matters in the hands of the Court for your consideration. The Prosecution submits that having regard to the evidence heard, all the evidence heard in this case, the Court has enough evidence before it to make a safe and sure finding beyond reasonable doubt that the accused is guilty, both under Articles 7(1) and Article 7(3), on all counts of the indictment as alleged. Thank you very much, Your Honours, for your patience. May it please you.
